transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-09
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Alex Nguyen (Redwood AE), Sana Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Lopez (Head of ML, BrightCart), Ethan Ford (Infra Eng), Priya Shah (CTO)

[00:00] Alex: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh quick check-in — looks like we got all five, Maya, Ethan, Priya, can you hear us okay?
[00:10] Maya: yes, loud and clear. thanks.
[00:12] Priya: yep good here.
[00:15] Alex: awesome. agenda today — quick recap of last week's benchmark, the sizing spreadsheet updates, then autoscaling policy options and burst planning, and finish with next steps. sound good?
[00:25] Ethan: sounds good. we've got our infra person on so we can dive into traces if needed.
[00:30] Sana: great. I'll start with a quick run-through of the benchmark we ran yesterday — it's the same POC workload you shared, 2k daily active users simulated, mixed chat + embeddings, 1k concurrent sessions at peak, and we did a 10-minute spike test up to 400 RPS.
[00:46] [01:00] Sana: baseline results — using the 30B open model variant on our Dedicated pool with 8x A100s (v4) equivalent, average token latency ~120ms, 95th ~420ms, 99th ~1.2s during spike windows. tail seems correlated with cold kv cache misses and prefix cache warming.
[01:25] Maya: okay 99th at 1.2s — our target is 95th <500ms for most user flows, sometimes 99th can be higher but that 1.2s is kind of in line with what we saw. do you think that's from cold starts?
[01:40] Sana: yeah mostly — the KV cache wasn't fully populated for the burst. we saw a lot of repeated prompts that benefit from prefix caching but the cache TTL was low in this run. also a couple of model context switches — switching between a quantized 8-bit variant and the full FP model caused extra overhead in a few requests.
[01:55] Ethan: quick Q — you mentioned 8x A100s equivalent. for BrightCart's Dedicated estimate what's the minimum cluster size we should reserve to meet sustained 200 RPS with room for bursts to 500?
[02:10] Alex: good question — high level, for sustained 200 RPS with the observed latencies we'd recommend reserving a 4 GPU pool with autoscale to 8 for bursts. that gives you headroom for warm pools and reduces queuing. but Sana, maybe you can explain the numbers?
[02:25] Sana: sure. from yesterday's telemetry a single A100-like instance can handle roughly 50 RPS for your workload at target latency if we optimize batching and use the quantized variant. so 4 GPUs -> ~200 RPS sustained. for bursts to 500 RPS we either scale to 10 GPUs or use burst capacity + prewarmed instances. because scaling cold can add 30-90s, we recommend keeping a small warm pool of 2-3 machines ready depending on cost tolerance.
[02:53] [03:00] Priya: that makes sense. cost is a concern — how do we trade off warm pool costs vs slightly higher 99th latencies during spikes?
[03:10] Alex: that's the core tradeoff. warm pools cost you committed resources, but they cut cold-start tail dramatically. we'll include specific numbers in the sizing sheet — e.g., warm pool of 2 GPUs increases monthly by X but reduces spike tail from ~1.2s to ~450ms in our tests.
[03:26] Maya: can you share the spreadsheet now? we've been looking at the earlier one but an updated one would help.
[03:30] Alex: we'll send an updated one after the call. action item.
[03:33] Sana: two autoscale approaches we recommend: request-based (RPS) autoscaling which watches queue depth / incoming requests, and kernel/infra-level GPU utilization autoscaling. combined approach tends to be best — RPS triggers scale-up quickly and utilization ensures we don't over-provision after burst.
[03:50] Ethan: what about cooldowns and scale-down behaviour — in ecom spikes can be very bursty, like 2-3 minutes then down. we don't want to ripple-scale and thrash.
[04:00] Sana: agreed. recommended policy: rapid scale-up threshold (e.g., 80% queue or >300 RPS sustained for 30s) with conservative scale-down (e.g., CPU/GPU utilization <40% for 5 minutes) plus minimum warm pool of 2 nodes. also set a max scale factor to avoid runaway costs.
[04:18] [05:00] Maya: can Redwood do warm pool prewarming and keep them on standby only billing for reserved capacity? how does billing look for Dedicated?
[05:10] Alex: Dedicated is reserved capacity billing; warm pools are effectively reserved VMs/GPUs so you pay for them like any dedicated instance. we can model scenarios — keep in mind we also support burst credits / transient burst slots for short spikes which are cheaper than full reserved. we'll call those "burst slots" in the sheet.
[05:30] Priya: is there an option to fall back to a cheaper quantized model automatically during extreme bursts? that would help latency and cost but may affect quality.
[05:42] Sana: yes, we support model fallbacks — routing policy can say: if queue depth > X or latency > Y, fallback to quantized-8b variant or smaller context window. quality degradation should be evaluated but often acceptable for low-stakes flows like simple product suggestions.
[05:55] Ethan: any data on how much throughput improves with 8-bit quantization for our model class?
[06:00] Sana: for the family you shared, quantization got us ~1.6-2x throughput at similar average latency but tail improved mainly because kernel memory pressure lowers. will include concrete numbers in the size sheet.
[06:12] [07:00] Maya: about KV / prefix cache — is there a recommended TTL? we have a lot of repeated prompts for returning users.
[07:20] Sana: TTL depends on user churn. for returning users a TTL of 24h gives great hit rates, but that increases memory footprint. we typically recommend adaptive TTLs: use longer TTL for high-frequency prefixes, shorter for long-tail. that's part of our Optimize suggestions.
[07:36] Alex: also we can shard prefix cache by user buckets to avoid eviction storms at peak.
[07:40] Priya: what about cold-start mitigation for new model variants? sometimes our team wants to roll a small change and we saw spikes.
[07:50] Sana: rollout strategy: canary small percent, prewarm canary nodes, and use traffic shadowing to prime KV caches before full rollout. we'll provide an example rollout config.
[08:03] [09:00] Ethan: we ran a small internal spike test last night and saw a queue depth spike — I can share logs. the puzzling bit was a 30s burst where 99th hit 1.5s even though average stayed low.
[08:18] Maya: yes that's the file we attached, the trace 2026-03-08-burst.log — Ethan will export the RPS/CDFs after the call.
[08:26] Alex: perfect, please send that. it'll help tune thresholds.
[08:30] Sana: one more note — our autoscaler supports prioritized queues so critical routes (checkout) can preempt less-critical ones (recommendations). that reduces user-facing latency for high-value flows.
[08:44] Priya: we like that — can you show how preemption looks in practice? is there a QoS token or priority header we set?
[08:52] Sana: yes, we expose per-route QoS tokens, and in the Dedicated config you can set route weights. we'll include a sample config snippet.
[09:00] [10:00] Maya: regulatory question — logs and audit trails, we need audit logs turned on for all inference requests for compliance. will that impact performance?
[09:14] Alex: audit logging is available; it's append-only and shipped to your KMS-secured S3. it adds a small overhead — usually <5% latency increase if synchronous. we recommend asynchronous logging to reduce impact, but you'll need to evaluate from compliance side.
[09:33] Ethan: on network side, can we keep everything inside our VPC? BrightCart requires private topology for production.
[09:41] Alex: yes Dedicated supports VPC peering and private deployment. for POC we ran in Redwood shared infra but production Dedicated will be provisioned in your VPC or via private link. we'll document the steps.
[09:55] [11:00] Priya: what's the suggested rollback policy if a model rollout increases error rates?
[10:03] Sana: automated rollback on error rate thresholds and latency regressions; we also support immediate manual cutover to previous model variant and traffic steering. canary + auto-rollback is standard.
[10:12] Maya: ok, timeline — assuming we get the sizing sheet and we run the 500 RPS spike next Tue, when can we expect the final recommendation?
[10:20] Alex: if we get traces by Wed and run the spike Tue, we'll aim to deliver final sizing + cost estimate by next Friday (2026-03-20).
[10:27] [12:00] Ethan: quick nit — during the spike test, what's the exact test harness to use so results are comparable to your benchmark?
[10:35] Sana: we'll share a k6 script and a sample payload set; key is to include warm-up, steady-state, and spike phases: 10m warm-up at 50% load, 10m steady at target, then 5-10m spike to 500 RPS, then cool-down. include repeating user prefixes to exercise KV hits.
[10:55] Maya: perfect.
[11:00] [13:00] Priya: any major blockers that you'd flag for procurement or security?
[11:08] Alex: from security side, we'll need SSO/SAML setup, SOC2 docs (we'll send), and KMS integrations for keys. procurement will ask for terms for Dedicated reserved capacity — we'll include a draft MSA and order form.
[11:26] Priya: okay procurement will review once we get draft.
[11:30] [14:00] Maya: last question on monitoring — can we get token-level cost by route in the console?
[11:38] Alex: yes, Console shows per-route token counts and cost breakdown, as well as latency heatmaps and trace links. we'll give you a short demo in the infra deep dive.
[11:50] Sana: and tracing hooks can be forwarded to your existing observability stack.
[12:00] [15:00] Alex: recap of next steps — Alex send sizing + pricing sheet, Sana send autoscale templates and k6 test harness, Ethan share RPS traces and run the spike test, schedule infra deep dive on 2026-03-12. agreed?
[12:20] Maya: agreed.
[12:25] Priya: agreed. thanks.
[12:28] Alex: thanks everyone — we'll follow up in email with the docs and invite for the deep dive.
[12:35] [45:30] meeting end: 15:46 UTC
